subject: physiology
title: Determinants of Cardiac Output, Inotropy, and Fick Principle

steps.tx: The total volume of blood pumped by each ventricle into the systemic or pulmonary circulation per minute is the **cardiac output**. Equal to stroke volume multiplied by heart rate, normal cardiac output measures approximately five litres per minute in a resting seventy-kilogram adult, indexing to three point zero litres per minute per square metre as the cardiac index.
steps.say: Cardiac output is stroke volume multiplied by heart rate, normally five litres per minute at rest, regulated by preload, afterload, inotropy, and heart rate.

nodes.label: Stroke Volume (mL/beat) x Heart Rate (bpm) = Cardiac Output (L/min)

steps.tx: The load the ventricle stretches against before it ejects has a name every clinician uses loosely. **Preload** is end diastolic stretch, set by venous return and filling pressure, and within limits more stretch means a stronger ejection by the Frank Starling mechanism. Diuretics, bleeding and venodilators all treat or cause disease through this one variable. Estimating it honestly at the bedside remains harder than defining it on paper.
steps.say: Preload is end diastolic stretch from venous filling, governing ejection strength by Frank Starling. Diuretics and bleeding act through it.

vis.alt: Image showing preload as ventricular filling and end diastolic stretch.
vis.caption: A filling ventricle stretches in diastole to set preload before ejection. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: The degree of stretch exerted on ventricular myocytes immediately prior to active contraction represents **preload**. Preload is clinically indexed by left ventricular end-diastolic volume or end-diastolic pressure. Governed by total blood volume, venous capacitance, and skeletal muscle pump activity, increased preload augments stroke volume via the Frank-Starling mechanism.
steps.say: Preload is the myocardial stretch at the end of diastole, indexed by end-diastolic volume and governed by venous return and circulating blood volume.

vis.alt: Venous return, central venous pressure, and preload determinants.
vis.caption: Preload regulation by venous return, circulating blood volume, and capacitance vessels. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: The mechanical load or resistance against which the ventricle must contract to eject blood is **afterload**. In the left ventricle, afterload is determined by systemic vascular resistance, aortic compliance, and left ventricular wall stress formulated by Laplace law. Elevating afterload, as in arterial hypertension or aortic stenosis, decreases stroke volume and increases myocardial oxygen demand.
steps.say: Afterload is the resistance opposing ventricular ejection, determined by systemic vascular resistance and wall stress, elevated in hypertension and stenosis.

left.title: Preload (Volume Load)
points: Tension in ventricular wall at end of diastole
Determined by venous return and total blood volume
Increases stroke volume via Frank-Starling law

right.title: Afterload (Pressure Load)
points: Tension in ventricular wall during active ejection
Determined by systemic vascular resistance and aortic impedance
Decreases stroke volume and prolongs isovolumetric phase
Reduced by pure arteriolar dilators (hydralazine, ACE inhibitors)

steps.tx: According to **Laplace law**, ventricular wall stress is directly proportional to intraventricular systolic pressure multiplied by internal chamber radius, divided by twice the myocardial wall thickness. Consequently, chronic pressure overload in aortic stenosis triggers concentric ventricular hypertrophy, thickening the myocyte wall to normalize wall stress, whereas chamber dilation in heart failure maladaptively escalates wall stress.
steps.say: Laplace law dictates that wall stress equals pressure times radius divided by twice the wall thickness. Concentric hypertrophy thickens walls to normalize stress.

nodes.label: Divided by 2 x Ventricular Wall Thickness (h)
Calculates Myocardial Wall Tension (Stress = P x r / 2h)
Concentric Hypertrophy Increases Thickness (h) to Preserve Normal Stress

steps.tx: Contractility is the variable in heart performance that loading conditions cannot explain. **Increased contractility** shifts the whole function curve upward, so the same preload ejects more blood when sympathetic drive or drugs strengthen each cross bridge cycle. It is measured imperfectly at the bedside and inferred from ejection speed and fraction. Failing hearts lose it progressively, which is why inotropes rescue temporarily while adding long term cost.
steps.say: Contractility is intrinsic ejection strength independent of loading, raised by sympathetic drive. Failing hearts lose it progressively.

vis.alt: Image showing contractility as the strength of ventricular contraction at a given preload.
vis.caption: A ventricle ejects more strongly at the same filling as contractility rises. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: The intrinsic contractile strength of the myocardium independent of alterations in preload and afterload is **contractility**, or inotropy. Positive inotropic agents such as adrenaline and digoxin increase intracellular calcium transients, accelerating cross-bridge cycling and shifting the Frank-Starling curve upward and to the left, generating larger stroke volumes from any given end-diastolic volume.
steps.say: Contractility is the intrinsic strength of contraction independent of preload or afterload, shifted upward by beta-agonists and digitalis.

vis.alt: Ventricular function curves illustrating positive and negative inotropic shifts.
vis.caption: Contractility shifts in ventricular performance curves under inotropic stimulation. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: The gold-standard physiological method for measuring cardiac output in humans is based on the **Fick principle**. Formulated by Adolf Fick, the principle states that the total uptake or release of a substance by an organ equals the blood flow through the organ multiplied by the arteriovenous concentration difference of that substance across the organ.
steps.say: The Fick principle calculates cardiac output: oxygen consumption divided by the arteriovenous oxygen concentration difference across the pulmonary circulation.

nodes.label: Sample Arterial Oxygen Content (CaO2): ~200 mL O2 per Litre
Sample Pulmonary Mixed Venous Oxygen (CvO2): ~150 mL O2 per Litre

steps.tx: Applying the Fick principle to cardiac output requires measuring whole-body oxygen consumption via spirometry, alongside arterial oxygen content from a peripheral artery and mixed venous oxygen content sampled from the pulmonary artery via a Swan-Ganz catheter. In an adult consuming two hundred and fifty millilitres of oxygen with an arteriovenous oxygen difference of fifty millilitres per litre, **pulmonary blood flow** equals five litres per minute.
steps.say: Applying Fick: 250 mL oxygen consumed divided by a 50 mL arteriovenous oxygen difference yields a cardiac output of five litres per minute.

rows: 50 mL O2 per litre of blood

steps.tx: In clinical practice, cardiac output is frequently measured via **thermodilution**. A known volume of cold saline is injected into the right atrium through a pulmonary artery catheter, and a thermistor at the catheter tip records downstream temperature changes in the pulmonary artery. The area under the resulting temperature-time curve is inversely proportional to cardiac output.
steps.say: Thermodilution injects cold saline into the right atrium and records temperature downstream; the area under the curve is inversely proportional to cardiac output.

left.title: Direct Fick Method
points: Invasive arterial and pulmonary artery blood sampling

right.title: Thermodilution Method
points: Uses cold saline indicator rather than oxygen
Inaccurate in severe tricuspid regurgitation or intracardiac shunts
